content: Maternity blues, also known as baby blues, is a condition that affects approximately 75-80% of mothers after childbirth. It is characterized by a range of symptoms, most commonly involving mild depression. It is important to note that baby blues is distinct from postnatal depression unless the symptoms are abnormally severe. After the delivery of the placenta, the hormonal production associated with pregnancy ceases abruptly. This results in significant hormonal changes, as the body experiences withdrawal from the extremely high levels of estrogen, progesterone, and endorphins that were present during pregnancy. These hormonal shifts are compounded by the physical, mental, and emotional exhaustion that often accompanies caring for a newborn, as well as the sleep deprivation that is typical during this period. Together, these factors contribute to the development of maternity blues. Additionally, it is normal for the ovaries, which have been largely inactive during the last six months of pregnancy, to take several weeks to resume their normal pre-pregnancy hormonal production. In some cases, this condition may also be associated with thyroid dysfunction. The symptoms of maternity blues include the following: Episodes of weepiness and sudden bouts of tears. Sudden and unpredictable mood swings. Heightened anxiety and hypersensitivity to criticism. Feelings of low mood and irritability. Difficulty concentrating and making decisions. A sense of feeling disconnected or unbonded with the baby. Restlessness and insomnia. In contrast to the baby blues, some women may experience a phenomenon referred to as baby pinks. This condition is characterized by an exaggerated and illogical sense of euphoria, akin to a mild to severe form of mania. However, these symptoms can sometimes serve as a precursor to an impending depressive imbalance, such as postnatal depression or postnatal psychosis.
